Spatial geometry and centrography

Source: vignettes/spatial-geometry.Rmd
spatial-geometry.Rmd

Distances, projections, centres, ellipses and the other geometry that spatial analysis of crime starts from.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws one. ?name gives the arguments and the value in full.

Great-circle distance

hvdist(): The distance along the sphere between pairs of points given in longitude and latitude. The central angle is computed as the atan2 of the cross and dot products of the two unit vectors, written so that nothing cancels: accurate to a few units in the last place from coincident points to antipodes (the spherical case of Vincenty 1975). The Earth is taken as a sphere of mean radius r; distances on the ellipsoid differ by up to about 0.5 per cent.

# Toronto to Montreal, metres
hvdist(c(-79.38, 43.65), c(-73.57, 45.50))
#> [1] 503922
pts <- data.frame(lon = c(0, 90, 180), lat = c(0, 0, 0))
hvdist(pts, c(0, 0))
#> [1]        0 10007557 20015114

Equal-area projection of longitude and latitude, and its inverse

eqproj(), eqinv(): eqproj() maps longitude and latitude to planar metres by the Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection of the sphere about a centre; eqinv() maps them back. Areas are exact, so intensities, nearest-neighbour expectations and K functions computed on the result are right; lengths are scaled by cos(c / 2) along the radius from the centre and its inverse across it (c the central angle), so within 100 km of the centre every length is right to 3.1e-5 relative. Every planar function of the package takes the projected coordinates; those with a lonlat argument call this projection themselves.

p <- eqproj(c(-79.40, -79.38, -79.35), c(43.64, 43.66, 43.65))
p
#>            x             y
#> 1 -1877.6518 -1111.6869087
#> 2  -268.1467  1111.9561852
#> 3  2145.5306     0.3446339
a <- attr(p, "centre")
eqinv(p, lon0 = a[1], lat0 = a[2])
#>      lon   lat
#> 1 -79.40 43.64
#> 2 -79.38 43.66
#> 3 -79.35 43.65

Mean centre and dispersion of points

cgstat(): The (weighted) mean centre of a point pattern, the standard deviations of the two coordinates, the standard distance deviation (the root mean squared distance from the mean centre), and the geometric and harmonic means of the coordinates (Bachi 1959; Neft 1966). The mean centre is the point that minimises the sum of squared distances to the points. The dispersions divide by the total weight less k: k = 1 makes the squared values unbiased for the variances; k = 2 is the convention of some crime-mapping texts; k = 0 divides by the total weight. That the mean centre minimises the weighted sum of squared distances is proved in Lean: see proof("cgstat").

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = rnorm(50, 100, 10), y = rnorm(50, 200, 5))
cgstat(p)
#>          w         mx         my         sx         sy        sdd         gx         gy 
#>  50.000000 101.004483 200.586632   8.313939   4.844140   9.622228 100.653418 200.529543 
#>         hx         hy 
#> 100.284986 200.472685
cgstat(p[, 1], p[, 2], w = rep(1:2, 25))
#>          w         mx         my         sx         sy        sdd         gx         gy 
#>  75.000000 100.685776 200.457192   8.553285   4.753294   9.785321 100.307901 200.401917 
#>         hx         hy 
#>  99.908680 200.346969
cgstat(p, k = 0)  # dispersions over n, not n - 1
#>          w         mx         my         sx         sy        sdd         gx         gy 
#>  50.000000 101.004483 200.586632   8.230380   4.795453   9.525520 100.653418 200.529543 
#>         hx         hy 
#> 100.284986 200.472685

Median centre of points

cgmedn(): The median of the x coordinates and the median of the y coordinates (the mean of the two middle values for an even number of points). It depends on the orientation of the axes: rotating the points does not rotate it. webpt() gives the rotation-invariant centre of minimum distance.

cgmedn(c(1, 2, 3, 10), c(5, 1, 2, 2))
#>   x   y 
#> 2.5 2.0

Centre of minimum distance

webpt(): The point c that minimises the weighted sum of distances sum(w * |p - c|) to the points: the Weber point or spatial median, which, unlike the median centre, does not depend on the axes. It is found by Weiszfeld’s iteration with the modification of Vardi and Zhang (2000), which keeps every step defined and the sum non-increasing when an iterate lands on a data point. The optimality gap certifies the answer: it is 0 exactly at a minimiser. The minimiser is unique unless all the points lie on one line with the weight split evenly.

webpt(c(0, 1, 0, 10), c(0, 0, 1, 10))
#>            x            y          obj          gap         iter         code 
#> 5.000000e-01 5.000000e-01 1.555635e+01 4.086973e-10 2.200000e+01 1.000000e+00

Standard deviational ellipse

sdell(): The ellipse whose axes lie along the eigenvectors of the weighted covariance matrix of the points about their mean centre, with semi-axes c times the square roots of its eigenvalues (Wang, Shi and Miao 2015). It is the ellipse of the rotated-axes formulas of Lefever (1926) and Ebdon (1988) once the same divisor is used; texts differ only in the divisor (k) and in the multiplier (some multiply by sqrt(2)). The curve of the standard deviation by direction that Lefever drew is not this ellipse (Gong 2002); the ellipse is returned. For bivariate normal points the ellipse with c = sqrt(-2 * log(1 - p)) covers a share p of them: c = 1 covers 39.3 per cent, c = 2 86.5 per cent. The parallel-axis identity behind the ellipse’s centre is proved in Lean: see proof("sdell").

set.seed(2)
x <- rnorm(200)
sdell(x, 0.5 * x + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3), c = 2)
#>            mx            my             a             b         angle          area 
#> -0.0007417526  0.0681841044  2.4146550213  0.5262845280  0.4870207069  3.9923220528

Convex hull of points

cvhull(): The smallest convex polygon holding every point, by Andrew’s monotone chain with an exact orientation predicate (Shewchuk 1997), so near-collinear points never make a wrong turn. Points on an edge are not vertices; of coincident points the first is reported.

cvhull(c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0.5), c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0.5))
#> $idx
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $area
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $perim
#> [1] 4

Nearest-neighbour index

nnidx(): The mean distance from each point to its k-th nearest neighbour, against its expectation under complete spatial randomness (CSR) in the rectangle win: the nearest-neighbour index of Clark and Evans (1954) and its k-order extension (Thompson 1956), with Donnelly’s (1978) edge-corrected expectation for the first order and, when nsim > 0, a Monte Carlo test against nsim patterns of as many uniform points in the rectangle. The Monte Carlo p-values have exact size; the z statistics ignore that nearest-neighbour distances are dependent and, uncorrected, the edge. The index tests only the k-th neighbour distances, not complete spatial randomness as a whole.

set.seed(1)
x <- runif(200)
y <- runif(200)
nnidx(x, y, win = c(0, 1, 0, 1), kmax = 3, nsim = 99)
#> $order
#>   k       mean        exp    ratio pclu preg         sd
#> 1 1 0.03753432 0.03535534 1.061631 0.84 0.17 0.01848106
#> 2 2 0.05462585 0.05303301 1.030035 0.44 0.57 0.01925094
#> 3 3 0.06778844 0.06629126 1.022585 0.19 0.82 0.01949659
#> 
#> $ce
#>  donnelly     ratio         z        zc 
#> 0.0364416 1.0299854 1.6674068 0.8361710 
#> 
#> $dist
#> NULL

Ripley’s K function

ripk(): Ripley’s K function of a point pattern in the rectangle win at radii r, and Besag’s L = sqrt(K / pi). Under complete spatial randomness K(r) = pi r^2 and L(r) = r. Four estimators: "none" (no edge correction), "border" (only points at least r from the edge are centres), "modif" (the modified border estimator, with the area of the eroded window; NaN once r reaches half a side) and "iso" (Ripley’s isotropic correction, each pair weighted by the inverse of the share of the circle through the other point that lies in the rectangle, computed exactly). The normalisation is n (n - 1), as in spatstat.

set.seed(1)
ripk(runif(100), runif(100), win = c(0, 1, 0, 1), r = seq(0, 0.25, 0.05))
#>      r           k          l
#> 1 0.00 0.000000000 0.00000000
#> 2 0.05 0.007686885 0.04946525
#> 3 0.10 0.033207387 0.10281167
#> 4 0.15 0.080766297 0.16033936
#> 5 0.20 0.131964756 0.20495289
#> 6 0.25 0.201545381 0.25328618

Envelopes of Ripley’s L function and a test of complete spatial randomness

ripenv(): L(r) - r for the data, its pointwise minimum, maximum and mean over nsim patterns of as many uniform points in the rectangle, and a global Monte Carlo test on the maximum absolute deviation T = max_r |L(r) - r|, whose p-value (1 + #{T_sim >= T}) / (nsim + 1) has exact size (Ripley 1977; Diggle 2013). The pointwise envelopes are not a test of the whole curve: each radius alone falls outside them with probability 2 / (nsim + 1) under randomness.

set.seed(1)
ripenv(runif(100), runif(100), win = c(0, 1, 0, 1),
       r = seq(0.01, 0.25, 0.02), nsim = 39)$test
#>          t          p 
#> 0.01033936 0.15000000

Fuzzy mode

fzmode(): For each point, the number of points (itself and coincident ones included) within distance r of it. With r = 0 it counts coincident points, the mode of exact locations; with r > 0 it is the fuzzy mode of the crime-mapping literature, a fixed-radius scan centred on each incident. Counts of nearby points overlap by design: each point counts its own neighbourhood.

fzmode(c(0, 0, 1, 5), c(0, 0, 0, 5), r = 1)
#> [1] 3 3 3 1

K-means partition of points

kmpart(): Partitions the points into k groups by Lloyd’s iterations: each point joins its nearest centre (the lowest-numbered on ties), then each centre moves to its points’ mean (upd = "mean", K-means, minimising the within-group sum of squares) or to their centre of minimum distance (upd = "weber", a spatial K-medians minimising the sum of distances), until no point changes group or after maxit moves. An emptied group keeps its centre. The result depends on the start: k-means++ seeding (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007), the centres of the busiest grid cells at least a given distance apart, or centres given.

set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(30, 0), rnorm(30, 5))
y <- c(rnorm(30, 0), rnorm(30, 5))
kmpart(x, y, k = 2, seed = 1)$cen
#>            x        y  n       ss       sd
#> 1 5.13277458 5.113333 30 40.91834 31.93770
#> 2 0.08245817 0.110278 30 51.51169 33.83318

Nearest-neighbour hierarchical clustering

nnhclu(): Groups points that lie closer together than a threshold distance, then groups the groups, order by order (after Johnson 1967, as used for crime hot spots). At the first order two points are linked when their distance is below the threshold: fixd, or the mean nearest-neighbour distance expected under complete spatial randomness in an area area plus z standard errors, 0.5 sqrt(A / m) + z sqrt((4 - pi) A / (4 pi)) / m for m units, with z = qnorm(p) (p = 0.5 gives the expectation itself, smaller p a stricter threshold). Points with a linked neighbour are taken in decreasing number of links; each one not yet clustered takes every unclustered point linked to it; groups of at least minpts points are kept. Their centres of minimum distance become the units of the next order, with the threshold recomputed for their number, while at least four remain, up to maxord orders. The iterative reassignment some descriptions add after the first pass is not done: its rule is not stated unambiguously.

set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(40, 0, 0.3), rnorm(40, 6, 0.3), runif(40, -5, 10))
y <- c(rnorm(40, 0, 0.3), rnorm(40, 6, 0.3), runif(40, -5, 10))
nnhclu(x, y, area = 225, p = 0.05, minpts = 5)$clusters
#>   order points units         mx           my         wx          wy         a         b
#> 1     1     40    40 0.03845448 -0.003796574 0.06246601 -0.03941408 0.2470327 0.2266867
#> 2     1     36    36 6.00748914  5.922730801 5.99404607  5.93418792 0.3063012 0.2568727
#> 3     1      5     5 6.13610851  6.711097797 6.09427553  6.66090240 0.1958946 0.0298542
#>      angle    thresh
#> 1 2.820476 0.6309155
#> 2 2.060319 0.6309155
#> 3 0.769340 0.6309155

Search-circle hot-spot areas

stacel(): Hot-spot areas from search circles (Block and Block 1995): circles of radius r are centred on the nodes of an nx by ny grid spanning the rectangle win (corners included), the points in each are counted, the circles holding at least two points are ranked by count and the first top are kept; kept circles that share a point are merged, repeatedly, and a hot-spot area is the set of points in a merged group, kept if it has at least minpts. Descriptions differ on the circle’s radius and on the grid; both are the caller’s choice here.

set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.2), runif(60, 0, 10))
y <- c(rnorm(30, 2, 0.2), runif(60, 0, 10))
stacel(x, y, win = c(0, 10, 0, 10), r = 0.75, top = 5, minpts = 5)$clusters
#>   points       mx       my       wx       wy         a         b     angle
#> 1     35 2.027899 2.025648 2.055272 2.024903 0.3233517 0.2532551 0.1950933

Risk-adjusted nearest-neighbour hierarchical clustering

rnnhcl(): Nearest-neighbour clustering (as nnhclu(), first order) with the threshold distance adjusted for a baseline population at risk, so that incidents dense only because people are dense there are not called a cluster. In nnhclu() the threshold is the mean nearest-neighbour distance under complete spatial randomness plus z standard errors, 0.5 sqrt(A / n) + z sqrt((4 - pi) A / (4 pi)) / n, which is f / sqrt(lambda) with lambda = n / A and f = 0.5 + z sqrt((4 - pi) / (4 pi n)). Here the uniform intensity is replaced by the intensity the n incidents would have if they followed the baseline: lambda_i = n b(p_i) / B, where b is the normal-kernel density (bandwidth h) of the baseline units with sizes bw and B is their total, and two incidents i and j are linked when |p_i - p_j| < f / sqrt((lambda_i + lambda_j) / 2). Taking the mean of the two intensities is this function’s reading of “the threshold at the pair’s baseline density” (the published description does not say how the two ends combine); a uniform baseline gives back nnhclu()’s threshold. Grouping is nnhclu()’s first order; higher orders are not formed.

set.seed(1)
town <- cbind(x = rnorm(400, 0, 1), y = rnorm(400, 0, 1))
inc <- rbind(town[1:60, ], cbind(x = rnorm(15, 3, 0.1),
                                 y = rnorm(15, 3, 0.1)))
r <- rnnhcl(inc, base = town, h = 0.5, minpts = 5)
r$clusters
#>   points       mx      my      wx       wy         a         b    angle
#> 1     15 2.973022 3.00705 2.97886 3.000247 0.1228748 0.1070088 1.886728

Head-bang smoothing

hdbang(): Smooths values at points or areal units (rates by area centroid, say) by Hansen’s (1991) head-bang rule, which removes isolated peaks and troughs while keeping edges between regions of different level. For each unit i the rule takes its nn nearest neighbours and every pair (j, k) of them whose angle at i is at least ang degrees, so that i lies roughly between j and k (a triple); with ntrip > 0 only the ntrip triples whose ends are nearest (smallest |p_j - p_i| + |p_k - p_i|) are kept. Each triple gives a low value min(v_j, v_k) and a high value max(v_j, v_k); the low screen is the median of the lows, the high screen the median of the highs, and the new value is the median of the low screen, v_i and the high screen, so v_i moves only if it lies outside both. With weights w (populations at risk, say) the screens are weighted medians, each end weighted by its own unit’s weight, after Mungiole, Pickle and Simonson (1999): the smallest value whose cumulative weight reaches half the total. A unit with no triple (on the outer edge of the points) keeps its value; Hansen’s extrapolated end triples are not formed. Each of iter passes starts from the previous pass’s values.

g <- expand.grid(x = 1:6, y = 1:6)
v <- rep(1, 36)
v[15] <- 50
hdbang(g, v = v)[15]
#> [1] 1

Correlated random walk of a series of events

crwalk(): Treats the successive locations of a series (incidents attributed to one offender, in time order) as a correlated random walk (Kareiva and Shigesada 1983): steps of independent lengths and changes of heading (turning angles) independent of each other and of the steps. The fit gives the mean and mean squared step and the mean cosine and sine of the turns; the expected squared displacement after k moves is Kareiva and Shigesada’s for symmetric turning (mean sine 0), k E l^2 + 2 (E l)^2 c / (1 - c) (k - (1 - c^k) / (1 - c)), next to the observed mean over every start. The walk is then continued nsim times for h steps from the last location and heading, each turn and step drawn independently and uniformly from the observed ones (an empirical correlated random walk), and the simulated positions summarise where the next events may fall. It describes movement; it does not identify anyone, and a series with few events gives a rough walk.

set.seed(1)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(20, 0, 0.5))
p <- cbind(x = cumsum(cos(a)), y = cumsum(sin(a)))
r <- crwalk(p, h = 3, nsim = 200, seed = 1)
r$fit
#>      steps         ml        ml2          c          s       head 
#> 19.0000000  1.0000000  1.0000000  0.8935287  0.1187582  1.9052388
r$msd
#>   k      obs      exp        x        y       sdx       sdy
#> 1 1 1.000000 1.000000 12.12662 10.09144 0.3882481 0.1794948
#> 2 2 3.787057 3.787057 11.60345 10.74197 0.7778394 0.4737584
#> 3 3 8.165410 8.170902 11.07326 11.25329 1.1794886 0.8584427

Mantel’s space-time test

mantst(): The Pearson correlation, over all pairs of events, between their spatial dissimilarity (the distance, or 1 / (distance + cs) when cs > 0, Mantel’s reciprocal transform) and their temporal one (|t_i - t_j|, or 1 / (|t_i - t_j| + ct)), with a permutation test that permutes the times over the fixed locations (Mantel 1967). Drawing distances and intervals independently instead, as some descriptions do, does not keep the dependence among the pairs of one distance matrix and gives no test of stated size. Memory grows with the number of events, not pairs; time with pairs times permutations.

set.seed(1)
x <- runif(60)
y <- runif(60)
mantst(x, y, t = x + rnorm(60, sd = 0.1), nsim = 199, seed = 1)
#>           r       pairs         pup         plo          p2 
#>    0.574889 1770.000000    0.005000    1.000000    0.005000

Spatial-temporal moving average

stmavg(): For each event, the mean centre of the span events centred on it in time order (ties in input order), the window shortened at the ends of the series. It traces how the centre of a series of incidents moves over time. It is a descriptive device of the crime-mapping literature with no original paper to cite; the mean centre is that of cgstat().

stmavg(x = 1:7, y = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13), t = 7:1, span = 3)
#>    mx        my n
#> 1 1.5  1.000000 2
#> 2 2.0  1.333333 3
#> 3 3.0  2.000000 3
#> 4 4.0  3.333333 3
#> 5 5.0  5.333333 3
#> 6 6.0  8.666667 3
#> 7 6.5 10.500000 2

Distance-decay functions for journey to crime

jtdecay(): The decay of the chance of offending with distance from an offender’s base, in the forms of Brantingham and Brantingham (1981), Rossmo (2000) and Levine (2009): "linear", f = max(0, A + B d), par = c(A, B); "negexp", f = A exp(-b d), par = c(A, b) with b >= 0; "normal", f = A dnorm(d, mu, s), par = c(A, mu, s); "lognormal", f = A dlnorm(d, mu, s), par = c(A, mu, s) (the lognormal density of d; some texts use log d^2 and 1 / d^2, which is not a density); "trunc", the truncated negative exponential, f = P d / dp up to the peak dp and P exp(-C (d - dp)) beyond, par = c(P, dp, C); and "table", values tab at distances 0, delta, 2 delta, …, linear in between and 0 beyond, par = delta (as jtcal() tabulates).

jtdecay(c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5), type = "trunc", par = c(1, 0.5, 0.8))
#> [1] 0.00000000 1.00000000 0.67032005 0.30119421 0.02732372

Journey-to-crime surface

jtsurf(): Ranks the cells of a grid as candidate bases of an offender from the locations of a series of incidents. mode = "sum" gives the classic aggregate surface, the sum over incidents of the decay of their distance to the cell (Canter et al. 2000; Levine 2009); mode = "lik" gives the sum of the logarithms, the log-likelihood of the cell as base when the decay function is the planar density of an incident about the base and the incidents are independent (O’Leary 2009), so that prob is the posterior over cells under a uniform prior. The sum surface is not a likelihood.

s <- jtsurf(c(2, 3, 4), c(2, 4, 3), win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), nx = 30,
            ny = 30, type = "negexp", par = c(1, 1), mode = "lik")
s$peak
#>  cell     x     y 
#> 467.0   3.3   3.1

Empirical distance decay from solved trips

jtcal(): A kernel density estimate of trip lengths from known offender trips, to calibrate a decay function (Levine 2009; Silverman 1986). With refl = TRUE the kernels are reflected at 0, so no mass falls below 0 and the estimate integrates to 1 over [0, Inf). Tabulated at evenly spaced distances it is a "table" decay for jtdecay() and jtsurf().

set.seed(1)
trips <- rexp(200, 1 / 2)
jtcal(trips, t = seq(0, 10, 0.5), h = 0.5)
#>  [1] 0.341941995 0.334326174 0.303888364 0.263429537 0.223093541 0.178452942 0.129191709
#>  [8] 0.095269714 0.079083025 0.063478487 0.046114240 0.036675173 0.025708978 0.013938566
#> [15] 0.006084284 0.003949455 0.004978870 0.005423329 0.005837164 0.005507356 0.003471230

Accuracy of a journey-to-crime surface on a solved series

jtacc(): Given a surface over the grid of jtsurf() and the offender’s known base: the surface’s value in the base’s cell, the hit score (the share of the grid searched, in decreasing order of the surface, up to and including the base’s cell), in the best and the worst order of ties (Rossmo 2000; Canter et al. 2000), and the error distance from the peak cell’s centre to the base.

s <- jtsurf(c(2, 3, 4), c(2, 4, 3), win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), nx = 30,
            ny = 30, type = "negexp", par = c(1, 1), mode = "lik")
jtacc(s$prob, win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), base = c(3.2, 2.9))
#>            p      hitbest     hitworst          err         peak         cell 
#>   0.00932350   0.01000000   0.01111111   0.22360680 467.00000000 437.00000000

Bayesian journey to crime

bjtc(): Combines a journey-to-crime surface over origin zones with an origin-destination matrix of solved offences (Levine 2009; Levine and Block 2011): P(Jtc), the surface; P(O), the origins of all solved offences; P(O|Jtc), the origins of offences in the zones where the series happened; their product, Bayes’ numerator with the surface as prior; and the risk, the product over P(O), renormalised. Each block sums to 1. The matrix describes past solved offences and inherits their selection.

od <- matrix(c(5, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1, 0, 1, 6), 3)
bjtc(pj = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), od = od, dest = c(1, 2, 2))
#>    pj   po  pod       prod       risk
#> 1 0.5 0.35 0.45 0.59210526 0.55900621
#> 2 0.3 0.30 0.45 0.35526316 0.39130435
#> 3 0.2 0.35 0.10 0.05263158 0.04968944

Circle hypothesis of a crime series

crchyp(): Canter and Larkin’s (1993) circle hypothesis: draw the circle whose diameter joins the two crime sites of a series that lie farthest apart. An offender whose home lies within it is a “marauder” (who travels out from home), one whose home lies outside a “commuter”. Gives the circle, the share of the sites it holds (all of them, unless the series is far from round) and, for each home given, whether it lies within.

crchyp(c(0, 4, 2), c(0, 0, 1), home = c(2, -1))
#> $centre
#> x y 
#> 2 0 
#> 
#> $r
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $pair
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> $share
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $mar
#> [1] TRUE

Hit score of a geographic profile

hitscr(): A geographic profile ranks the cells of a search area; searched from the highest score down, the hit score is the share of the area searched before the offender’s home is reached (Rossmo 2000), the smaller the better. Cells scored the same as the home cell are counted both ways: hit searches them after the home, hitt before it.

hitscr(c(0.9, 0.5, 0.7, 0.5, 0.1), home = 2)
#>   home above ties rank hit hitt
#> 1    2     2    2    3  40   80

Spatial weights

spwt(): Builds the neighbours and weights the autocorrelation statistics (gearc(), gorg(), lmorn(), locgi()) use: the k nearest neighbours of each point (type = "knn", ties broken by the lower row number), the points within distance d ("band", the distance itself included), or a contiguity list nb ("contig", one element per unit giving its neighbours’ numbers, as spdep’s poly2nb() returns). Weights are 1, or the inverse distance to the power idw; style = "row" divides each unit’s weights by their sum (a unit without neighbours keeps none), "raw" leaves them.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(20), y = runif(20))
w <- spwt(p, k = 3)
str(w)
#> List of 5
#>  $ n: int 20
#>  $ i: int [1:60] 1 1 1 2 2 2 3 3 3 4 ...
#>  $ j: int [1:60] 12 16 19 5 11 14 13 16 17 6 ...
#>  $ d: num [1:60] 0.347 0.353 0.24 0.179 0.317 ...
#>  $ w: num [1:60] 0.333 0.333 0.333 0.333 0.333 ...
spwt(nb = list(2, c(1, 3), 2), type = "contig")$w
#> [1] 1.0 0.5 0.5 1.0

Geary’s C

gearc(): Geary’s (1954) contiguity ratio of values on units with spatial weights w: C = (n - 1) sum w_ij (x_i - x_j)^2 / (2 S0 sum (x_i - xbar)^2), 1 under no autocorrelation, below 1 when neighbours are alike. Its variance is given under normality and under randomisation (Cliff and Ord 1981), with z statistics (1 - C) / sd and their upper normal tails, and, with nsim > 0, a permutation p-value against positive autocorrelation. That C has expectation 1 under randomisation is proved in Lean: see proof("gearc").

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(50), y = runif(50))
gearc(p[, 1] + p[, 2] + rnorm(50, sd = 0.1), spwt(p, k = 4))
#>            c           vn           vr           zn           zr           pn 
#> 9.221870e-02 9.592157e-03 9.036261e-03 9.268791e+00 9.549637e+00 9.413378e-21 
#>           pr        pperm           s0 
#> 6.507588e-22          NaN 5.000000e+01

The general G of Getis and Ord

gorg(): The global concentration statistic of Getis and Ord (1992) for non-negative values: G = sum_ij w_ij x_i x_j / sum_{i != j} x_i x_j, its expectation S0 / (n (n - 1)) and variance under randomisation, the z statistic, its upper normal tail (high values near high values) and, with nsim > 0, a permutation p-value. Unlike Moran’s I and Geary’s C it tells high-value clusters from low-value ones. Its expectation under randomisation is proved in Lean: see proof("gorg").

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(50), y = runif(50))
gorg(exp(3 * p[, 1]), spwt(p, type = "band", d = 0.2, style = "raw"))
#>            g            e            v            z            p        pperm 
#> 1.663958e-01 1.167347e-01 1.514881e-04 4.034852e+00 2.731842e-05          NaN

Local Moran (LISA)

lmorn(): Anselin’s (1995) local indicator of spatial association for each unit: with z = x - mean(x) and m2 = mean(z^2), I_i = z_i / m2 sum_j w_ij z_j, its expectation and variance under total randomisation, the two-sided normal p-value, and a conditional permutation p-value: unit i keeps its value and its neighbours’ values are drawn without replacement from the others, nsim times from seed. The quadrant tells high-high and low-low clusters from high-low and low-high outliers. The p-values are per unit and not adjusted for the many tests made (use stats::p.adjust()); with row-standardised weights the sum of the I_i is S0 times global Moran’s I. That identity is proved in Lean: see proof("lmorn").

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60), y = runif(60))
v <- ifelse(p[, 1] > 0.7 & p[, 2] > 0.7, 5, 1) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3)
l <- lmorn(v, spwt(p, k = 5), nsim = 199, seed = 1)
head(l)
#>            ii           e         v          z         p pperm quad
#> 1 -0.08136911 -0.01694915 0.1668323 -0.1577177 0.8746793 0.290    4
#> 2  0.12229676 -0.01694915 0.1668323  0.3409120 0.7331698 0.215    2
#> 3  0.03723394 -0.01694915 0.1668323  0.1326550 0.8944662 0.480    2
#> 4  0.14258312 -0.01694915 0.1668323  0.3905786 0.6961088 0.095    2
#> 5  0.18202573 -0.01694915 0.1668323  0.4871449 0.6261557 0.255    2
#> 6  0.09264972 -0.01694915 0.1668323  0.2683280 0.7884469 0.390    2

Local G and G* of Getis and Ord

locgi(): The local statistics of Getis and Ord (1992) as z values (Ord and Getis 1995): G_i compares the weighted sum of the neighbours’ values with its expectation from the other n - 1 values; G*_i (star = TRUE) includes the unit itself with weight 1 and uses all n. Large positive values mark concentrations of high values, large negative ones of low values. With star = TRUE the weights are best binary (style = "raw").

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60), y = runif(60))
v <- rpois(60, ifelse(p[, 1] > 0.7, 6, 2))
locgi(v, spwt(p, type = "band", d = 0.2, style = "raw"))
#>  [1]  0.23994257 -1.19393804 -0.85693776  4.16902467 -1.51580855  2.62650766  3.78952137
#>  [8]  0.87555456 -0.91284462 -1.74706652 -2.08423675 -0.89182354  1.19393804 -1.51232152
#> [15]  1.27896346 -0.37705262  2.28529782  2.46318889 -0.23878761  2.08423675  4.04305111
#> [22] -1.05904046  0.55717109 -2.22803818 -0.07959587 -0.72460663 -1.06343180 -0.56842821
#> [29]  2.08423675 -0.73778305 -0.72460663 -0.91284462 -0.72460663 -0.75790427  2.30828021
#> [36]  1.28199634  1.78732733 -1.97494476  2.30828021 -0.56071512  2.09530386  1.19393804
#> [43]  1.03474630  0.30383766 -1.72790811  1.03289627 -1.17365736 -1.62693646  1.44921325
#> [50]  0.78034560 -0.65203187  2.50225827 -1.44605478 -2.08423675 -1.51918828 -1.17365736
#> [57] -1.03474630 -0.91485098 -0.23878761 -0.55738971

Directional mean and circular variance

dirmn(): The mean direction of a set of directions, the mean resultant length R (from 0, directions spread evenly, to 1, all the same), the circular variance 1 - R and the circular standard deviation sqrt(-2 log R) (Mardia and Jupp 2000). Directions are given as angles, or as points seen from an origin (the directions of incidents from an offender’s base, say). The mean direction of points depends on the origin chosen. That R lies in [0, 1] is proved in Lean: see proof("dirmn").

dirmn(c(1, 2, 0), c(1, 1, 3), origin = c(0, 0))
#>      theta    bearing          r        var         sd          w          n 
#>  0.9315290 36.6273216  0.8948002  0.1051998  0.4714971  3.0000000  3.0000000
dirmn(angle = c(0.1, 0.2, 6.2))
#>        theta      bearing            r          var           sd            w 
#>  0.072363804 85.853859466  0.993136769  0.006863231  0.117361758  3.000000000 
#>            n 
#>  3.000000000

Local Getis-Ord Gi* on a grid of counts

gstr(): The local statistic Gi* of Getis and Ord (1992; Ord and Getis 1995) for each cell of a grid of counts, with binary weights on the cells within rad cell widths (rad = 1.5: the 3 by 3 block, cell included), its normal p-value and Benjamini-Hochberg q-value, a conditional permutation p-value, and an exposure-aware version: given the total, the count of a neighbourhood is binomial with the neighbourhood’s share of the exposure under complete spatial randomness, so cells overhanging the study area neither inflate the mean nor get flagged. No threshold is applied.

set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(rpois(100, 2), 10)
m[4:5, 4:5] <- 9
g <- gstr(m)
g[g$qe < 0.05, ]
#>    row col       gz           pz           qz  pp       ze           pe           qe
#> 34   4   4 4.374058 1.219581e-05 0.0006097906 NaN 5.368464 2.971884e-06 0.0001485942
#> 35   5   4 4.186330 2.835012e-05 0.0009450040 NaN 5.138058 7.201663e-06 0.0002400554
#> 44   4   5 4.374058 1.219581e-05 0.0006097906 NaN 5.368464 2.971884e-06 0.0001485942
#> 45   5   5 3.998602 6.371769e-05 0.0015929423 NaN 4.907652 1.698365e-05 0.0004245913

Andresen’s spatial point pattern test

sptst(): Compares where two point patterns fall over the same areal units (Andresen 2009): for each unit, the difference between its share of the test pattern b and its share of the base pattern a, with a bootstrap p-value from multinomial resamples of each pattern; the S index is the share of units whose difference is not significant (1: the patterns are alike everywhere).

set.seed(1)
a <- rpois(30, 10)
b <- rpois(30, 10)
sptst(a, b, nboot = 199, seed = 1)$glob
#>        left       empty        elig     flagged           s           z           p 
#>   0.0000000   0.0000000  30.0000000   2.0000000   0.9333333  -0.4188539   0.4464579 
#>       nboot 
#> 199.0000000
